text.en: Imagine a big screen showing smiling children from different states, each proudly showing you a craft from their home. That is exactly what happens in this chapter. It opens with a short passage about India and then takes you into the Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat programme.

Bharat has been known across the world as a land of wise and heroic people. Its rich and varied culture has attracted travellers since ancient times. The people here live in unison, which means together in harmony. This shows unity in diversity to the world. Bharat has rivers, lakes and high mountains, and green forests with many plants, insects, birds and animals. These keep the country prosperous and respected. The advice to everyone is that, as inhabitants, we need to keep working hard so that Bharat continues to prosper.
In the story, a teacher asks students in a big hall if they are ready to meet friends from all over the country. The programme is called Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat. Renu explains that it is to know that we all belong to one nation and share a bond, and that our unity in diversity makes us a wonderful country. The programme aims to improve interaction and mutual understanding between people of different states and union territories by pairing them. It celebrates unity in diversity and strengthens emotional bonds. It aims to give people a sense of common identity by sharing best practices and experiences, and to contribute to nation building by showing how connected our cultures are.
Akanksha from Uttarakhand tells about Aipan, a folk art drawn on family functions and festivals. It is done with white rice flour paste on brick-red walls coloured with geru, a red clay. It is made on floors and walls of puja rooms and outside the main door. It is an art made by the women of the family. The designs are beautiful and mathematical and based on cultural traditions and observations of nature.
Priyaranjan from Odisha belongs to a tribe that practises Dhokra, a four-thousand-year-old metal craft. First a figure is made of clay and dried, then covered with a layer of wax and the fine details are carved on the wax. The figure is covered with clay and put in the fire. The wax melts and flows out through small openings. Then melted brass scrap is poured into the empty space and takes the shape of the wax. At last the outer clay is removed and the metal figure is finished.
Chitra from Kerala describes coconut shell craft. First a brown coconut shell is cleaned inside and out, then made smooth with sandpaper or a machine. Next it is shaped as wished and a base is fixed so that it is stable. At last it is polished with wood polish to make it shine. Bowls, household things and even jewellery are made. It is a biodegradable craft, which means it will not harm the environment.
Balamurali from Kondapalli village tells about a four-hundred-year-old toy-making art. Soft wood from nearby hills is used. Each part of the toy is carved separately and pieces are joined with makku, a paste of tamarind seed powder and sawdust. Details are added and finally the toys are coloured with oil and watercolours or vegetable dyes and enamel paints. The toys show folk stories, animals, birds, bullock carts and rural life. Kondapalli toys and coconut shell craft both use natural materials from nature.
To give steps in order, use to begin, first, then, next, after that, finally and at last. Example: first I get up, then I wear my uniform, next I eat, after that I wear my shoes, and finally I pick up my bag. The children speak in the simple present tense, which tells about regular actions. With he, she and it we add s or es to the verb. Examples: I know how to dance, he speaks very loudly, she draws paintings, they practise spellings on Friday.
Speak about a local art form of your region such as painting, rangoli, metal craft, embroidery, music, dance or drama. Say its name, what is needed and how it is made, using first, after that, next, then and at last. Write a paragraph of five sentences about the art form you liked best and give your reasons. Madhubani painting is a traditional art form from Bihar. Natural colours can be made from haldi for yellow, leaves for green, flowers or geru for red, and indigo for blue. In the listening passage, gakkad bharta is made by roasting dough balls and brinjal and tomatoes, then serving crumbled gakkad with bharta and ghee.

problem.en: Put the steps of making a Dhokra figure in order.

text.en: Start with the clay figure and wax layer.

why.en: The first stage makes the model.

text.en: Carve details, cover with clay, fire it so wax melts, pour in melted brass, and finally remove the clay.

why.en: Pouring brass in the place of wax is the key step.

problem.en: Write present tense sentences with he, she, it: she / draw / paintings.

text.en: With she we use the verb with s or es.

why.en: Third person singular needs an s.

text.en: She draws paintings in free periods.

prompt.en: Choose one craft from the chapter and explain how it is made, using sequence words.

requiredIdeas.en: Name the craft and the state.
Describe the steps with first, next, then and finally.
Say what is made from it.

commonMisconceptions.en: All the crafts are made by machines.
Aipan is made on paper with paint.

points.en: Bharat is rich in culture, rivers, forests and people who live in unison.
Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat celebrates unity in diversity through state pairing.
Aipan, Dhokra, coconut shell craft and Kondapalli toys are traditional crafts.
Sequence words show the order of steps.
The present tense tells about regular actions, and he, she, it take s or es.
